newsitem.title: USA: U.S. tax bill details being written, some dropped.
newsitem.headline: U.S. tax bill details being written, some dropped.

text.p: Final details of a tax cut package were being ironed out Wednesday with one education provision dropped and tax credits for the Amtrak railroad system tied to other changes.
Congressional Republicans and the White House earlier this week reached agreement on the five-year, $94 billion net tax cut package. Congress is scheduled to vote on the bill Thursday.
As the vote neared, an education tax break provision aimed at parents with children in elementary and high schools was eliminated after President Clinton threatened a veto, lawmakers said.

Inability to reach compromise in another area would likely leave Amtrak unable to access new funds in the tax bill and a Caribbean trade provision kept out of the legislation, Senate Republican aides said.

The five-year tax package includes $2.3 billion in tax credits for Amtrak, but the money would not be available to the national rail system until a comprehensive package of labour and other reforms was approved.
Republicans offered a trade off to include a provision sought by the White House called the Caribbean Basin Initiative (CBI) in exchange for including the Amtrak reform package the Republicans want.
Senate aides said the White House rejected the Republican Amtrak proposal late Tuesday and it appeared neither proposal would be included in the tax bill.
The CBI would allow those countries trade provisions similar to countries in the North American Free Trade Agreement.
Meanwhile, Republican legislators released a letter from Clinton to House Speaker Newt Gingrich that was delivered Tuesday night on the education provision.

At issue was a proposal by Sen. Paul Coverdell, a Georgia Republican, which would have allowed parents to contribute $2,000 a year after-tax to an education account, similar to an Individual Retirement Account. The interest earned on that money would be tax-free if used for the child's education.

"As you know, in working out the final agreement, I strongly opposed the Coverdell amendment," Clinton wrote in the letter dated Tuesday. "I would veto any tax package that would undermine public education by providing tax benefits for private and parochial school expenses," the letter said.
Coverdell said after the letter threatening a veto was delivered, his proposal was dropped from the bill. "I don't believe any of us would have the whole (tax bill) go down with it," Coverdell said.

On Amtrak, Republicans had made four proposals, the most controversial of which would require the railroad to negotiate under prevailing labour laws the severance pay and benefits with laid-off workers and allow Amtrak to contract out work. By law, the rail line is obligated to pay six years severance.
The proposal would also have required a vote by Congress on any liquidation of Amtrak and would have chosen a new board of directors.
